title: This Bird Sings With Its Wings, 107 Times a Second

scenes.text: This bird sings, but not with its throat.
The club-winged manakin of the Andes. The male lifts his wings and knocks them together 107 times a second.
Twice a hummingbird's wingbeat. One feather has seven ridges. Another rakes across them.
Each ridge is struck twice. Fourteen knocks a cycle, 107 cycles a second: a violin note near 1,500 vibrations a second.
To do it, the bird evolved solid wing bones. Most birds have hollow ones, which make flying easier.
Heavier bones on every flight, for one note to impress a female. Watch it sing with its wings.

description:
The male club-winged manakin of Colombia and Ecuador makes a violin-like tone by knocking its wings together about 107 times a second, more than twice a hummingbird's wingbeat.
One secondary feather carries seven ridges that another feather strikes, producing a tone of about 1,500 cycles per second, and the bird has solid wing bones instead of the hollow bones most birds use for flight. Discovered by Cornell's Kimberly Bostwick.
What is the strangest bird song you've heard?
subject: club-winged manakin
first_comment: Solid bones, just to play one note. Which bird has the most unusual courtship you know?
